claims.text: Overall wear resistance in FeNiCrCoCu HEA thin coatings during high-temperature sliding is governed by the in situ formation of a thin, adherent oxide layer.
Microscopic deformation in FeNiCrCoCu HEA thin coatings during high-temperature sliding is governed by the in situ formation of a thin, adherent oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer is enriched in Cr and Cu.
The oxide layer protects the coating against abrasive wear.
The oxide layer suppresses plastic deformation during sliding.
A higher-temperature or longer-duration post-deposition anneal will increase oxide-scale stability.
Post-deposition thermal treatment will produce a thicker oxide scale than the baseline as-deposited condition.
Post-deposition thermal treatment will produce a more crystalline oxide scale than the baseline as-deposited condition.
Post-deposition thermal treatment will produce a more adherent oxide scale than the baseline as-deposited condition.
Thermal treatment enhances oxidation of Cr and Cu at grain boundaries and at the coating surface.
The resulting oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding.
The resulting oxide layer limits microcrack initiation.
The resulting oxide layer distributes the applied load more uniformly.
The thermally treated coating will have a lower wear rate than the as-deposited coating under otherwise identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
The thermally treated coating will exhibit less microscopic deformation than the as-deposited coating under otherwise identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
The as-deposited baseline coating forms only a minimal or less stable oxide layer during high-temperature sliding.
The predicted behavior is expected to hold during sliding at 600–800 °C, where oxidation kinetics are significant.
The predicted behavior may not apply during room-temperature sliding or in environments having substantially different oxidation kinetics.
